974.title: Harar, the walled city
974.hook: the walled city of Ethiopia, crowded with mosques and saints' shrines
974.howItsDone: In Harar, people visit the shrines of the city's saints, and Muslims pray in its many small mosques inside the old wall.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Swahili coast, where traders waited for the wind to turn. Your line was towns of the monsoon.

After dark, outside the old wall of a hilltop city in eastern Ethiopia, a man sits on the ground with a basket of scraps and calls out names. Out of the night come hyenas. He feeds them, sometimes from a stick held in his teeth. In this city, people say, the hyenas and the townsfolk have an old agreement: the animals are fed, and they leave the people alone. Inside the wall, the lanes twist, the houses are painted in bright colors, and every few turns there's another small mosque or the tomb of a holy man. Today: Harar.
screen: `HYENAS FED AFTER DARK.` → `AN OLD WALL ON A HILL.` → `LANES FULL OF MOSQUES AND TOMBS.`

segments.voice: Ethiopia has a long Christian history, and also a Muslim story reaching back to the first refuge, when early Muslims found safety with the king of Abyssinia. Sahih al-Bukhari even records that when that king died, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told his companions and led a funeral prayer for him. Harar grew up later, in the highlands of the east, as a Muslim trading town and a center of learning. Its old city is closed in by a wall with gates, and inside, the town is thick with mosques, shrines and tombs. Tradition calls Harar the city of saints. The saints here are the awliya, the friends of God: scholars and holy people whose graves are cared for, visited and prayed beside. Tradition also names a founding saint, Sheikh Abadir, said to have come from Arabia and settled the town. Muslims differ about visiting saints' tombs. Sufi tradition treasures it as a way of honoring the friends of God; other Muslims hold that prayer belongs at the mosque and that visits to graves should be kept simple. Harar holds a strong Sufi tradition, and its shrines are part of the city's life. Hararis have their own language too, Harari, once written in Arabic letters. A walled city with its own tongue and its own saints, in a land where churches and mosques have stood side by side for a very long time.

Say it softly, let it sit on the breath in and the breath out, and bring to mind one person you'd like to greet with peace, maybe someone it's hard to greet. If you pray, ask peace for them; if not, simply hold the word and the person together.

975.title: Nana Asma'u
975.hook: the poet and scholar of Sokoto who trained women teachers across the region
975.howItsDone: In northern Nigeria, Nana Asma'u's poems are still recited, and women's study circles that trace themselves to her yan taru meet to learn together.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Harar, the walled city in the Ethiopian highlands. Your line was the city of saints.

A woman sets out from her village on foot, wearing a tall, wide hat that marks her out on the road. She is walking to the city to learn. There she will memorize a set of poems: about the Prophet, about prayer, about the women saints of Islam, about how to live. Then she will walk home, gather the women of her village, and teach them every line. She is a jaji, a teacher. And the woman who trained her, who wrote many of those poems and sent teachers like her across the countryside, was the daughter of a reformer in what is now northern Nigeria. Today: Nana Asma'u.
screen: `A TALL HAT ON THE ROAD.` → `POEMS LEARNED BY HEART.` → `CARRIED HOME TO THE VILLAGE.`

segments.voice: Nana Asma'u was the daughter of Shehu Usman dan Fodio, a scholar and reformer whose movement founded the Sokoto Caliphate in West Africa. She grew up in a house full of books, learned the Qur'an by heart, and became a scholar in her own right. She wrote poetry in Arabic and in the local languages, Fulfulde and Hausa, so that people who didn't read Arabic could still learn. Her problem was a practical one. Women in the villages around Sokoto wanted to learn their faith, but they couldn't easily leave home and family for long. So she turned the problem around. Instead of bringing every woman to the city, she trained teachers, the jajis, who came to her, learned the lessons, and carried them back. The women who gathered around them were called the yan taru, the ones who come together. And she wrote the lessons as poems, because a poem is easy to remember and easy to pass on by mouth. Behind it all stood a simple conviction. The Qur'an teaches a short prayer, in Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge." And a hadith in Sunan Ibn Majah says that seeking knowledge is a duty on every Muslim. Nana Asma'u took that duty to include the women of the villages. She could not teach them all. She trained the teachers. Her poems are still recited in the region today.

976.title: Islam in Africa today
976.hook: the adhan sounds from Dakar to Mombasa, across a continent of Muslims
976.howItsDone: Across Africa, Muslims answer the adhan at each time of prayer in mosques large and small, and recordings of African reciters are shared and listened to around the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nana Asma'u of Sokoto, who sent her lessons out in verse. Your line was she trained the teachers.

Dawn on the Indian Ocean, in Mombasa, Kenya. A voice rises from a minaret: Allahu akbar. The light moves west, and the call moves with it: to Khartoum and Cairo along the Nile, across the Sahel to Kano and the old towns of the Niger, and at last to Dakar, on the Atlantic. Different accents, different melodies, the same words. A continent of mosques, some of them with stories you've walked through over these last days. Today: Islam in Africa today.
screen: `DAWN IN MOMBASA.` → `THE CALL MOVES WEST.` → `DIFFERENT VOICES, THE SAME WORDS.`

segments.voice: Africa's story with Islam began with refugees welcomed in Abyssinia in the Prophet's own lifetime. And the voice that carried the call to prayer in Medina has an African story too. A hadith in Sunan Abi Dawud tells how the words of the adhan came to a companion in a dream, and the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told him to teach them to Bilal, because Bilal's voice carried. Bilal, remembered by tradition as a man of Abyssinian descent, freed from slavery, stood up and called the believers to prayer. The same words are called today. And Islam in Africa is not one thing. It's the Sufi orders of Senegal, with their great gatherings. It's Qur'an schools in northern Nigeria where children sit with wooden boards. It's al-Azhar in Cairo, teaching students from many countries. It's the stone mosques of Lamu and the mud mosque of Djenné. It's recitation: Egyptian reciters like Abdul Basit Abd al-Samad and Mahmoud Khalil al-Husary, whose recordings are still played far beyond Egypt. The Qur'an names this kind of variety as one of God's signs. In Pickthall's translation, among His signs is "the difference of your languages and colours." Africa prays in Wolof, Hausa, Swahili, Somali, Amharic and Arabic, and stands in the same rows. That closes the part on Africa: the first refuge, Egypt and the Nile, the Sahara, Mali and Mansa Musa, Timbuktu, Djenné, Songhay, the Swahili coast, Harar, and Nana Asma'u.

Don't try to understand every word: listen to the breath between the verses, and let your own breath slow to meet it. If you pray, let the recitation carry you; if not, simply listen, the way you'd listen to the sea.

977.title: Persian and faith
977.hook: Persian becomes a great language of Islamic poetry: Sa'di, Attar, Hafiz
977.howItsDone: Persian poetry by Hafiz, Sa'di, Attar and Rumi is read, recited and memorized in Iran, Afghanistan and beyond, and some families keep the custom of opening Hafiz's collection at random for guidance.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the adhan, carried across a whole continent. Your line was africa prays. Today the road turns to Persia.

In a tea house in Shiraz, a thick book of poems sits on the table. Someone opens it at random, reads the first lines their eye lands on, and the whole table leans in to hear what it says about the week ahead. The poems are by Hafiz, and some families in Iran still keep this custom: a book of verse treated almost like a friend you can ask for advice. And those poems are in Persian, not Arabic. A new part of the path begins here: Persia, the Turks and the great empires. It begins with a language. Today: Hafiz.
screen: `A BOOK OF POEMS ON THE TABLE.` → `OPENED AT RANDOM.` → `A NEW PART: PERSIA AND THE TURKS.`

segments.voice: When Islam came to Persia, the language of the Qur'an and of prayer was Arabic, and it stayed that way. Muslims in Iran still pray in Arabic today. But Persian did not disappear. It came back as a written language, now in a script borrowed from Arabic and full of Arabic words, and it became a language for poets of the Muslim world. Three names lead the way through the next days. Attar, who wrote of birds on a long journey. Sa'di of Shiraz, who wrote stories and sayings about how people treat each other. And Hafiz, also of Shiraz, whose short love poems are read more than one way at once: as songs about human love and wine, and, by some readers, as poems of longing for God. His pen name is the title Muslims give someone who knows the Qur'an by heart. The Qur'an pays attention to language too. It calls itself, in Pickthall's translation, "a Lecture in Arabic, that ye may understand." Another verse says every messenger was sent with the language of his own people, to make the message clear to them. For these poets, faith did not need one language only. Prayer stayed in Arabic. Wonder, longing, jokes, advice and grief could come in Persian. One more detail: Hafiz's collection, as tradition has it, opens on a half-line of Arabic, and then the poem turns into Persian. Two languages, in one breath. The language of poets.

978.title: Attar's birds
978.hook: The Conference of the Birds, where thirty birds seek their king and find themselves
978.howItsDone: Attar's Conference of the Birds is read and taught in Sufi circles and Persian literature classes as an allegory of the seeker's journey to God, and it is often staged as theater and retold for children.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hafiz and the Persian poets, and your line, the language of poets.

All the birds of the world gather for a meeting. They have no king, and they've decided they need one. A small bird with a crest on its head steps forward: the hoopoe. A king exists, it tells them, far away behind a great mountain, and its name is the Simorgh. The road is long and dangerous. Who will come? Then, one by one, the excuses. The nightingale can't leave the rose it loves. The duck can't leave the water. The hawk is happy serving a human king. Each reason sounds perfectly sensible. This is the opening of a long Persian poem by Attar. Today: Attar's birds.
screen: `THE BIRDS WANT A KING.` → `THE HOOPOE KNOWS THE WAY.` → `ONE BY ONE, THE EXCUSES.`

segments.voice: The poem is called Mantiq al-Tayr, often translated the Conference of the Birds, or the Speech of the Birds. The title echoes the Qur'an, where Solomon says he has been taught the speech of birds. And the hoopoe is no random choice: in the Qur'an's story, a hoopoe brings Solomon news of the Queen of Sheba. So Attar's guide already carried messages in scripture. The hoopoe answers every excuse with a story, and slowly the birds set out. The way, the poem says, crosses seven valleys: the search, love, knowledge, detachment, unity, bewilderment, and finally poverty and annihilation. Many birds turn back. Many die on the road. Only thirty arrive. Then the turn. In Persian, thirty birds is si morgh. The king they searched for is the Simorgh. When the curtain lifts, they look at the Simorgh and see themselves; they look at themselves and see the Simorgh. Readers in the Sufi tradition hear in this the soul's journey to God, where the seeker who has let go of self finds the One sought was nearer than imagined. What that means has been argued over. In the poem, the Simorgh speaks of itself as a mirror, and many Sufi readers stress that the birds do not become God: what shines in a mirror is not the mirror. Some link it to the verse in Pickthall's translation: "We are nearer to him than his jugular vein." A long road, to find what was close all along. Thirty birds.
screen: `A HOOPOE GUIDES, AS IN THE QUR'AN.` · `SEVEN VALLEYS, MANY TURN BACK.` · `SI MORGH: THIRTY BIRDS.` · `THEY SEE THE KING, AND THEMSELVES.` · then, large: `THIRTY BIRDS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you're searching for right now: peace, purpose, God, or simply a better way to live this year. Then ask the hoopoe's question, what is my excuse, the rose I can't leave or the water I'm comfortable in, and name it honestly, without scolding yourself. If you pray, hold your search before God in your own words.

979.title: Sa'di of Shiraz
979.hook: the poet of Shiraz, whose lines say that humans are limbs of one body
979.howItsDone: Sa'di's Gulistan is a classic of Persian schooling, and his lines on the children of Adam are memorized and quoted across Iran and the Persian-speaking world.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Attar's birds, the thirty who reached the Simorgh and saw themselves. Your line was thirty birds.

A stubbed toe. That's all it takes. One small toe meets the leg of a table, and suddenly the whole of you is involved. Your hands grab your foot. Your face twists. Your voice says something you'd rather your grandmother hadn't heard. Nobody in your body says, that's the toe's problem. A poet from Shiraz took that ordinary fact and turned it into a Persian poem about every human being on earth. Today: Sa'di of Shiraz.
screen: `A STUBBED TOE.` → `THE WHOLE BODY RESPONDS.` → `A POET TURNS IT OUTWARD.`

segments.voice: Sa'di is remembered for two books: the Bustan, the orchard, in verse, and the Gulistan, the rose garden, in prose with poems woven through. The Gulistan is full of short stories about kings and beggars, judges and dervishes, travelers and fools, each ending with a lesson that often stings a little. Sa'di was a traveler himself. In one of his own stories, he is taken prisoner far from home and put to work digging a trench, until an acquaintance pays to set him free. He knew what it was to be a stranger. In the Gulistan comes the poem, here in paraphrase. The children of Adam are limbs of one another, made from one essence. When the world gives pain to one limb, the other limbs cannot rest. And if you feel nothing at the suffering of others, you do not deserve to be called human. The picture was not new. A saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari, describes believers in their mercy and love for one another as one body: when one part aches, the whole body answers with sleeplessness and fever. Sa'di's poem, many readers note, widens that body to all the children of Adam. Not only my family. Not only my faith. Anyone made of the same clay. A poem about strangers, written by a man who had been one, and built on a body that can't ignore its own toe. Limbs of one body.
screen: `THE ORCHARD AND THE ROSE GARDEN.` · `A TRAVELER WHO WAS ONCE A PRISONER.` · `THE CHILDREN OF ADAM ARE LIMBS.` · `THE BELIEVERS ARE ONE BODY.` · then, large: `LIMBS OF ONE BODY.`

segments.voice: Notice your own body for a moment, feet, hands, chest, all of it answering to all of it. Then picture one stranger you'll likely pass today, the person at the register or a neighbor whose name you don't know, and see them as a limb of the same body you belong to. If you pray, ask for their good; if not, simply wish it.
Sa'di. The Persian poet of Shiraz, of the Bustan and the Gulistan, who wrote that the children of Adam are limbs of one another. Today's word.

980.title: The Seljuks
980.hook: Turkish sultans who rule Persia and Anatolia and build the caravanserais
980.howItsDone: Muslims treat hospitality to guests and travelers as a religious duty, and Seljuk caravanserais in Turkey and Iran are visited today as monuments of that tradition.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sa'di, and the children of Adam as limbs of one another. Your line was limbs of one body.

A stone gateway stands on a dry plateau in central Anatolia, taller than a house, carved with patterns as fine as lace. It looks like the entrance to a palace. It was built for tired merchants and their animals, at the end of a long day on a road where the night is cold and not always safe. Behind it: a courtyard with a well, a small mosque, stables for the animals, rooms for the people. The gate shuts at night, and inside, everyone sleeps. Buildings like this still stand along the old roads, and some go back to one dynasty of Turkish sultans. Today: the Seljuks.
screen: `A STONE GATE ON A PLATEAU.` → `BUILT FOR TIRED MERCHANTS.` → `A ROOF FOR THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The Seljuks began as a family of Turkish tribesmen from Central Asia, Muslims, who moved west with their horses and herds. In time they ruled much of Persia and Iraq. When their leader Tughril entered Baghdad, the Abbasid caliph was still there, honored as the head of the Sunni world, but without real power. Tughril ruled with the title sultan, one who holds authority. So a new pattern took shape: the caliph as the symbol, the sultan as the ruler. Under the Seljuks, the vizier Nizam al-Mulk built the madrasahs you met earlier on this path. Later, a branch of the family ruled Anatolia from the city of Konya, the land where Rumi would live and teach. Along Anatolia's trade roads, the Seljuk sultans and their officials built caravanserais, road houses for travelers. Some were paid for by endowments, so a traveler could rest without paying for the night, and the animals were fed too. Why spend fortunes in stone on strangers? Trade, certainly: safe roads meant rich cities. But hospitality was also a duty of faith. The Qur'an names the wayfarer, the traveler on the road, among those who have a right to charity. And a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in Sahih al-Bukhari, links believing in God and the Last Day with honoring one's guest. A carved gate, a well, a mosque, a stable: faith built into a wall. The road houses.
screen: `TURKISH TRIBES BECOME SULTANS.` · `THE CALIPH REIGNS, THE SULTAN RULES.` · `KONYA, AND THE ANATOLIAN ROADS.` · `A PALACE FOR THE CARAVAN.` · then, large: `THE ROAD HOUSES.`

segments.voice: Think of one traveler in your own life: a friend driving in from far away, a new coworker, a delivery driver on a long shift. What would a road house look like for them, in your terms: a glass of water, a chair, a charger, a ride? If you pray, you can ask for the safety of travelers.
The Seljuks. Turkish sultans who ruled Persia and Anatolia, kept the caliph as a symbol, and built road houses, caravanserais, for travelers. Today's word.
Your line: the road houses. A gate for the night, and a right for the wayfarer. Day nine hundred eighty, done.
